result.topic_en: Example II (§17): from the sines of arcs nΦ, (n+1)Φ, (n+2)Φ, … in arithmetic progression, Euler expresses the arc Φ as an interpolation series, evaluates the infinite-product coefficients using his integral formula for such products, and obtains a series for Φ∫x^n dx(1−x)^{n−1}.
result.transcription:
$)$ 170 $($

Exemplum II.

§. 17. Si arcus a, b, c, d, etc. progressionem arithmeticam quamcunque constituant, vt sit
$a=n\Phi,\ b=(n+1)\Phi,\ c=(n+2)\Phi,\ d=(n+3)\Phi,$ etc.
ex eorum sinibus longitudinem arcus $\Phi$ definire.
Solutio generalis ante exhibita pro hoc casu dat
$\Phi=\frac{\sin.n\Phi}{n}\cdot\frac{(n+1)^2}{1(1+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+2)^2}{2(2+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+3)^2}{3(3+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+4)^2}{4(4+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+5)^2}{5(5+2n)}$ etc.
$-\frac{\sin.(n+1)\Phi}{n+1}\cdot\frac{n^2}{1(1+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+2)^2}{1(3+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+3)^2}{2(4+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+4)^2}{3(5+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+5)^2}{4(6+2n)}$ etc.
$+\frac{\sin.(n+2)\Phi}{n+2}\cdot\frac{n^2}{2(2+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+1)^2}{1(3+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+3)^2}{1(5+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+4)^2}{2(6+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+5)^2}{3(7+2n)}$ etc.
$-\frac{\sin.(n+3)\Phi}{n+3}\cdot\frac{n^2}{3(3+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+1)^2}{2(4+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+2)^2}{1(5+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+4)^2}{1(7+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+5)^2}{2(8+2n)}$ etc.
$+\frac{\sin.(n+4)\Phi}{n+4}\cdot\frac{n^2}{4(4+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+1)^2}{3(5+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+2)^2}{2(6+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+3)^2}{1(7+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+5)^2}{1(9+2n)}$ etc.
Ad valores horum productorum in infinitum excurrentium inuestigandos ponamus breuitatis gratia
$\Phi=\mathfrak{A}\frac{\sin.n\Phi}{n}-\mathfrak{B}\frac{\sin.(n+1)\Phi}{n+1}+\mathfrak{C}\frac{\sin.(n+2)\Phi}{n+2}-\mathfrak{D}\frac{\sin.(n+3)\Phi}{n+3}+$ etc.
et hi coefficientes sequenti modo inter se comparentur:
$\frac{\mathfrak{B}}{\mathfrak{A}}=\frac{nn}{(n+1)^2}\cdot\frac{2(2+2n)}{1(3+2n)}\cdot\frac{3(3+2n)}{2(4+2n)}\cdot\frac{4(4+2n)}{3(5+2n)}$ etc.
qui valor reducitur ad $\frac{nn}{(n+1)^2}\cdot\frac{(i+1)(2+2n)}{1(i+2+2n)}$ [?], denotante $i$ numerum infinitum, sicque erit $\frac{\mathfrak{B}}{\mathfrak{A}}=\frac{2nn}{n+1}$. Simili modo colligitur:
$\frac{\mathfrak{C}}{\mathfrak{B}}=\frac{1(1+2n)}{2(3+2n)}\cdot\frac{(n+1)^2}{(n+2)^2}\cdot\frac{(i-1)(4+2n)}{1(i+2n)}$ [?] $=\frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{2n(n+2)}$;
tum vero porro
$\frac{\mathfrak{D}}{\mathfrak{C}}=\frac{(n+2)(2n+2)}{3n(n+3)},\quad \frac{\mathfrak{E}}{\mathfrak{D}}=\frac{(n+3)(2n+3)}{4n(n+4)}$,
et sic deinceps; vnde sequitur fore
$\mathfrak{B}=\frac{2nn}{(n+1)}\mathfrak{A}$

$)$ 171 $($

$\mathfrak{C}=\frac{2n(2n+1)}{1\cdot2(n+2)}\mathfrak{A}$
$\mathfrak{D}=\frac{2n(2n+1)(2n+2)}{1\cdot2\cdot3(n+3)}\mathfrak{A}$
$\mathfrak{E}=\frac{2n(2n+1)(2n+2)(2n+3)}{1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot4(n+4)}\mathfrak{A}$
etc.
sicque totum negotium redit ad inuentionem primae litterae:
$\mathfrak{A}=\frac{(n+1)^2}{1(2n+1)}\cdot\frac{(n+2)^2}{2(2n+2)}\cdot\frac{(n+3)^2}{3(2n+3)}\cdot\frac{(n+4)^2}{4(2n+4)}$ etc.
Iam dudum autem demonstraui, huius producti generalis
$\frac{a(b+c)}{b(a+c)}\cdot\frac{(a+d)(b+c+d)}{(b+d)(a+c+d)}\cdot\frac{(a+2d)(b+c+2d)}{(b+2d)(a+c+2d)}$ etc.
valorem ita exprimi, vt sit
$=\frac{\int x^{b-1}dx(1-x^d)^{\frac{c-d}{d}}}{\int x^{a-1}dx(1-x^d)^{\frac{c-d}{d}}}$
vtraque scilicet integratione a termino $x=0$ ad $x=1$ extensa. Quare cum pro nostro casu sumi oporteat
$a=n+1;\ b+c=n+1,\ b=1,\ c=n,$ et $d=1$,
habebimus:
$\mathfrak{A}=\frac{\int dx(1-x)^{n-1}}{\int x^n dx(1-x)^{n-1}}=\frac{1}{n\int x^n dx(1-x)^{n-1}}$
hincque sequentem pro arcu $\Phi$ expressionem:
$\Phi\int x^n dx(1-x)^{n-1}=\frac{1}{nn}\sin.n\Phi-\frac{2n}{1(n+1)^2}\sin.(n+1)\Phi$
$+\frac{2n(2n+1)}{1\cdot2(n+2)^2}\sin.(n+2)\Phi-\frac{2n(2n+1)(2n+2)}{1\cdot2\cdot3(n+3)^2}\sin.(n+3)\Phi$
$+\frac{2n(2n+1)(2n+2)(2n+3)}{1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot4(n+4)^2}\sin.(n+4)\Phi+$ etc.
Quae series eo maiorem attentionem meretur, quod formulam integralem $\int x^n dx(1-x)^{n-1}$ inuoluit.

Y 2 Corol-

items.quote:
Si arcus a, b, c, d, etc. progressionem arithmeticam quamcunque constituant, vt sit
$a=n\Phi,\ b=(n+1)\Phi,\ c=(n+2)\Phi,\ d=(n+3)\Phi,$ etc.
ex eorum sinibus longitudinem arcus $\Phi$ definire.
items.english: If the arcs a, b, c, d, etc. form any arithmetic progression, so that a = nΦ, b = (n+1)Φ, c = (n+2)Φ, d = (n+3)Φ, etc., to determine the length of the arc Φ from their sines.

items.quote: Iam dudum autem demonstraui, huius producti generalis
items.english: But I have long since demonstrated that the value of this general product can be expressed as the ratio of the integrals ∫x^{b-1}dx(1−x^d)^{(c−d)/d} and ∫x^{a-1}dx(1−x^d)^{(c−d)/d}, both taken from x=0 to x=1.
